title: Client-knowable constraints stop becoming requests
outcome: A form does not accept what the request schema would reject, and the one form that hand-writes its own schema no longer diverges from the one the server enforces.
acceptanceCriteria: A blank opponent name stays accepted. The premise that it round-trips to a generic failure was tested against the real payload and is false: the request schema's z.string() takes an empty string, and every surface that renders a team name already falls back to 對手. There is no constraint to stage earlier, so none is added.

The forms that use a request schema as their resolver are left alone. The player create and edit forms already do this, which is the shape this decision points at; only the game forms hand-write a second definition.

Where the game form's schema was looser than the request schema it is tightened to match, but only where the control already enforces it: both team names become required strings, and the set count becomes the three values the radio group offers. No user-visible behaviour changes; what changes is that deriving the form schema later becomes a no-op instead of a behaviour change.

The divergences left in place are recorded rather than fixed: the form's optional id is not checked as an ObjectId, and phase, division and category are string enums the body converts. Neither is reachable through the UI, and both disappear when the form schema is derived rather than written.
The existing drift test gains the opposite direction. It proved the form can submit something valid; it now also proves the form blocks what the server would reject.
